humanities_role_explanation: Humanities subjects (e.g., History, Philosophy, World Religions) provide the raw question items, but the benchmark primarily tests generic multiple-choice question answering and factual recall under translation, rather than domain-specific hermeneutic, interpretive, or methodological inquiry.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Text-only multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects translated into 42 languages, supplemented with human-annotated cultural sensitivity metadata.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Tests multiple-choice question answering demanding factual recall of historical, philosophical, and religious knowledge, alongside cultural reasoning to evaluate the impact of Western-centric geographical and cultural biases.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Evaluates models across 57 diverse subjects, spanning STEM, Humanities, Social Sciences, and other domains.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates 14 open and closed models including GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Aya Expanse, and Command R+.

quantitative_metrics.note: Uses multiple-choice accuracy, ChrF++ for translation quality, and measures rank/position shifts across different subsets.

published_after_march_2023.note: Published as a preprint in February 2025.

summary: This paper introduces Global-MMLU, an enhanced version of the MMLU benchmark translated into 42 languages with professional and community annotations to address linguistic and cultural biases. The authors categorize questions into culturally-sensitive and culturally-agnostic subsets, revealing that 28% of MMLU questions require Western-centric cultural or regional knowledge. They evaluate leading LLMs on these subsets, demonstrating that cultural bias significantly distorts model performance rankings across different languages.
key_findings: 28% of MMLU questions require culturally-sensitive knowledge, with 86.5% of those tagged as Western-specific and 84.9% of geographic questions focusing on North America or Europe. Evaluating models on culturally-sensitive vs. culturally-agnostic subsets leads to an average of 5.7 rank changes and 7.3 position shifts across evaluated languages. Furthermore, models perform better on machine-translated data for low-resource languages but human-translated data for high-resource languages.
facets_explanation: Global-MMLU adapts the pre-existing MMLU dataset, which derives its ground truth from academic exam answer keys, requiring substantial external domain knowledge to answer correctly. Although the benchmark categorizes items into culturally sensitive and agnostic subsets, it maintains a single universal correct answer per item across its multilingual translations. Disagreements among the human annotators who labeled the cultural sensitivity of the questions were resolved using a majority voting scheme, filtering out minority interpretations.
results_explanation: The paper does not report a quantified human baseline or a single headline score for the best-performing model in the text, but presents evaluations across models in bar charts (Figures 9, 10, 11). It reports a systematic cultural asymmetry, finding that 'progress on MMLU depends heavily on learning Western-centric concepts, with 28% of all questions requiring culturally sensitive knowledge.' It also notes that performance systematically degrades on low-resource languages: 'performance declines significantly for low-resource languages... accompanied by an increase in performance variability, with the standard deviation rising for mid-resource languages and even more so for low-resource languages, particularly on CS datasets.'
